claim: The NH2-terminal domain (NTD; residues 1–66) of budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae Rad51 protein contains three SQ motifs (S2Q, S12Q, and S30Q; Woo et al., 2020).
source: We reported previously that the NH2-terminal domain (NTD; residues 1–66) of budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae Rad51 protein contains three SQ motifs (S2Q, S12Q, and S30Q; Woo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Woo et al., 2020

claim: The S/T-Q motifs, comprising S or T followed by Q, are the target sites of DNA damage sensor protein kinases ATM, ATR, and DNA-PK.
source: The S/T-Q motifs, comprising S or T followed by Q, are the target sites of DNA damage sensor protein kinases, that is ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated), ATR (RAD3-related) (Craven et al., 2002; Kim et al., 1999) and DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) (Traven and Heierhorst, 2005; Cheung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Mec1 and Tel1 are the budding yeast homologs of mammalian ATR and ATM, respectively.
source: Mec1 (Mitotic Entry Checkpoint 1) and Tel1 (TELomere maintenance 1) are the budding yeast homologs of mammalian ATR and ATM, respectively.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge with supporting citations

claim: Budding yeast lacks a DNA-PK homolog.
source: Budding yeast lacks a DNA-PK homolog (Craven et al., 2002; Kim et al., 1999; Menolfi and Zha, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The clustering of three SQ motifs within a stretch of 31 amino acids in Rad51-NTD fulfills the criteria to define an S/T-Q cluster domain (SCD).
source: This clustering of three SQ motifs within a stretch of 31 amino acids in Rad51-NTD fulfills the criteria to define an S/T-Q cluster domain (SCD; Traven and Heierhorst, 2005; Cheung et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on established criteria from cited literature

claim: The three SQ motifs of Rad51-NTD are phosphorylated in a Mec1- and Tel1-dependent manner during vegetative growth and meiosis.
source: The three SQ motifs of Rad51-NTD are phosphorylated in a Mec1- and Tel1-dependent manner during vegetative growth and meiosis.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the authors' previous work

claim: Mec1/Tel1-dependent NTD phosphorylation antagonizes Rad51 degradation via the proteasomal pathway, increasing the half-life of Rad51 from 30 min to ≥180 min.
source: Mec1/Tel1-dependent NTD phosphorylation antagonizes Rad51 degradation via the proteasomal pathway, increasing the half-life of Rad51 from 30 min to ≥180 min (Woo et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Mec1 and Tel1 exhibit an essential function in regulating protein homeostasis (proteostasis) in S. cerevisiae.
source: supporting the notion that Mec1 and Tel1 exhibit an essential function in regulating protein homeostasis (proteostasis) in S. cerevisiae (Corcoles-Saez et al., 2018; Corcoles-Saez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: A unifying definition of an SCD is having ≥3 S/T-Q sites within a stretch of 50–100 amino acids.
source: A unifying definition of an SCD is having ≥3 S/T-Q sites within a stretch of 50–100 amino acids (Traven and Heierhorst, 2005; Cheung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Mec1/Tel1-dependent phosphorylation of Rad53-SCD1 and Hop1-SCD specifically recruits and activates their downstream DNA damage checkpoint kinases Dun1 and Mek1, respectively.
source: For example, Mec1/Tel1-dependent phosphorylation of Rad53-SCD1 (residues 1–29) and Hop1-SCD (residues 258–324) specifically recruits and activates their downstream DNA damage checkpoint kinases Dun1 and Mek1, respectively (Lee et al., 2008; Carballo et al., 2008; Chuang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Dun1 phosphorylates three serine residues (S56, S58, and S60) of the ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor Sml1, subsequently promoting Sml1 ubiquitination and degradation via the 26 S proteasome.
source: Dun1 phosphorylates three serine residues (S56, S58, and S60) of the ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor Sml1, subsequently promoting Sml1 ubiquitination by the E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme Rad6 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase Ubr2, as well as promoting Sml1 degradation via the 26 S proteasome (Zhao and Rothstein, 2002; Uchiki et al., 2004; Andreson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Mek1 phosphorylates two Rad51 accessory factors, Rad54 and Hed1, suppressing Rad51's strand-exchange activity and preventing Rad51-mediated DSB repair, respectively.
source: Mek1 phosphorylates two Rad51 accessory factors, Rad54 and Hed1 (a meiosis-specific inhibitor of Rad51), suppressing Rad51's strand-exchange activity and preventing Rad51-mediated DSB repair, respectively (Niu et al., 2009; Callender et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Many SCD-containing proteins are neither targets of ATM/Tel1 or ATR/Mec1 nor functionally linked to DNA Damage response or DNA repair.
source: There are many other SCD-containing proteins that are neither targets of ATM/Tel1 or ATR/Mec1 nor functionally linked to DNA Damage response or DNA repair (Traven and Heierhorst, 2005; Cheung et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: SCDs often are intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in their native states due to their high percentages of STQ amino acid content.
source: Interestingly, due to their high percentages of STQ amino acid content, SCDs often are intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in their native states rather than adopting stable secondary and/or tertiary structures (Traven and Heierhorst, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: A common feature of IDRs is their high content of serine (S), threonine (T), glutamine (Q), asparagine (N), proline (P), glycine (G) or charged amino acids.
source: A common feature of IDRs is their high content of serine (S), threonine (T), glutamine (Q), asparanine (N), proline (P), glycine (G) or charged amino acids [arginine (R), lysine (K), and histidine (H)] (Romero et al., 2001; Uversky, 2019; Macossay-Castillo et al., 2019; Uversky et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: IDRs are key components of subcellular machineries and signaling pathways because they have the potential to associate with many partners due to their multiple possible metastable conformations.
source: Functionally, IDRs are key components of subcellular machineries and signaling pathways because they have the potential to associate with many partners due to their multiple possible metastable conformations.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about IDR function

claim: Many IDRs are regulated by alternative splicing and post-translational modifications.
source: Many IDRs are regulated by alternative splicing and post-translational modifications.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about IDR regulation

claim: Some IDRs are involved in the formation of various membraneless organelles via intracellular liquid-liquid phase separation.
source: Some IDRs are involved in the formation of various membraneless organelles via intracellular liquid-liquid phase separation (Wright and Dyson, 1999; Posey et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Highly charged IDRs can act as entropic bristles that enhance the water solubility but not the steady-state levels of their partner proteins when translationally fused.
source: Highly charged IDRs can act as entropic bristles that, when translationally fused to their partner proteins, only enhance the water solubility but not the steady-state levels of their partner proteins (Santner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Seven Q-rich motifs of S. cerevisiae proteins, including Rad51-NTD, have high STQN or STQ amino acid contents and exhibit autonomous expression-enhancing activity.
source: In this study, we first report that seven Q-rich motifs of S. cerevisiae proteins, including Rad51-NTD (Woo et al., 2020), have high STQN or STQ amino acid contents and exhibit autonomous expression-enhancing activity for high-level production of native protein and when fused to exogenous target proteins, for example β-galactosidase (LacZ), in vivo.
evidence: Stated as a finding from this study

claim: N-terminal fusion of Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH increased both steady-state levels of LacZ-NVH fusion proteins and β-galactosidase activities in vivo.
source: We confirmed that the N-terminal addition of Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH increased both steady-state levels of LacZ-NVH fusion proteins (Figure 1A) and β-galactosidase activities in vivo (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: Yeast Rad53-SCD1, Hop1-SCD, Sml1-NTD1–50 and Sml1-NTD1–27 exhibit protein expression-enhancing (PEE) activities.
source: Here, we further report that yeast Rad53-SCD1, Hop1-SCD, Sml1-NTD1–50 (residues 1–50) and Sml1-NTD1–27 (residues 1–27) also exhibit protein expression-enhancing (PEE) activities (Figure 1A and B, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: The Sml1 protein in the SK1 strain harbors three S/T-Q motifs (S4Q, S14Q and T47Q), whereas that in the S288c strain only has one SQ motif (S4Q, C14Q and T47M).
source: The Sml1 protein in the SK1 strain harbors three S/T-Q motifs (S4Q, S14Q and T47Q), whereas that in the S288c strain only has one SQ motif (S4Q, C14Q and T47M).
evidence: Stated as a factual observation about protein sequences

claim: The Q-rich motifs of three yeast prion-causing proteins (Sup35-PND, Ure2-UPD, and New1-NPD) exhibit PEE activities.
source: We found that the Q/N-rich NTDs of Sup35, Ure2 and New1 also display PEE activities, i.e., the prion nucleation domain (PND; residues 1–39) of Sup35 (Tuite, 2000), the Ure2 prion domain (UPD) (residues 1–91) (Wickner et al., 2004; Wickner, 1994), and the New1 prion domain (NPD; residue 1–146) (Shewmaker et al., 2007; Figure 1A and B, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: Sup35-PND containing 3 S, 12Q, 18 N, and an S17Q motif exerts critical functions in promoting [PSI+] prion nucleation.
source: Sup35-PND containing 3 S, 12Q, 18 N, and an S17Q motif exerts critical functions in promoting [PSI+] prion nucleation (Toombs et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The UPD of the Ure2 nitrogen catabolite repression transcriptional regulator is the basis of the prion [URE3+].
source: The UPD of the Ure2 nitrogen catabolite repression transcriptional regulator is the basis of the prion [URE3+] (Wickner et al., 2004; Wickner, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The UPD is critical for Ure2's function in vivo because its removal in the corresponding Ure2-ΔUPD mutants elicits reduced protein stability and steady-state protein levels.
source: The UPD is critical for Ure2's function in vivo because its removal in the corresponding Ure2-ΔUPD mutants elicits reduced protein stability and steady-state protein levels (but not transcript levels) (Shewmaker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Ure2-UPD adopts a completely disordered structure.
source: Ure2-UPD contains 10 S, 5T, 10Q, and 33 N, adopting a completely disordered structure (Ngo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: New1 is a non-essential ATP-binding cassette type F protein that fine-tunes the efficiency of translation termination or ribosome recycling.
source: New1 is a non-essential ATP-binding cassette type F protein that fine-tunes the efficiency of translation termination or ribosome recycling (Kasari et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The NPD of New1 supports [NU+] and is susceptible to [PSI+] prion induction.
source: The NPD of New1 supports [NU+] and is susceptible to [PSI+] prion induction (Santoso et al., 2000; Osherovich and Weissman, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: N-terminal fusion of Sup35-PND, Ure2-UPD or New1-NPD to LacZ-NVH all increased steady-state protein levels and β-galactosidase activities in vivo.
source: Here, we applied the LacZ-NVH fusion protein approach to show that N-terminal fusion of Sup35-PND, Ure2-UPD or New1-NPD to LacZ-NVH all increased steady-state protein levels (Figure 1A) and β-galactosidase activities in vivo (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: N-terminal fusion of Rad53-SCD1 to four different NVH-tagged target proteins (LacZ, GST, GSTnd, and GFP) all resulted in higher protein production in vivo.
source: We found that N-terminal fusion of Rad53-SCD1 to four different NVH-tagged target proteins (Figure 1C) or Rad51-ΔN (Figure 1D) all resulted in higher protein production in vivo.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D

claim: The PEE function is not affected by the quaternary structures of target proteins.
source: In conclusion, our results indicate that the quaternary structures of the target proteins (i.e. GFP, GSTnd, GST, LacZ and Rad51-ΔN) are irrelevant to the autonomous PEE activity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with different target proteins

claim: The autonomous PEE function of Rad51-NTD could be fully rescued in rad51-ΔN by N-terminal fusion of Rad53-SCD1, Rad53-SCD1-5STA or Sup35-PND.
source: Interestingly, the autonomous PEE function of Rad51-NTD could be fully rescued in rad51-ΔN (Supplementary file 1) by N-terminal fusion of Rad53-SCD1, Rad53-SCD1-5STA (all five S/T-Q motifs changed to AQs) or Sup35-PND, respectively.
evidence: Stated as an experimental finding

claim: The three yeast mutants (rad53-SCD1-rad51-ΔN, rad53-SCD1-5STA-rad51-ΔN and sup35-PND-rad51-ΔN) produced similar steady-state levels of Rad51-ΔN fusion proteins and exhibited high MMS resistance.
source: Compared to WT yeast cells, the three corresponding yeast mutants (rad53-SCD1-rad51-ΔN, rad53-SCD1-5STA-rad51-ΔN and sup35-PND-rad51-ΔN) not only produced similar steady-state levels of Rad51-ΔN fusion proteins (Figure 1D), but they also exhibited high MMS resistance (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E

claim: The addition of WT and mutant Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH did not affect the average copy number of the corresponding CEN-ARS plasmids in exponentially growing S. cerevisiae cells.
source: We found that the addition of WT and mutant Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH not only did not affect the average copy number of the corresponding CEN-ARS plasmids in exponentially growing S. cerevisiae cells (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The addition of Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH reduced the steady-state transcript levels of the corresponding LacZ-NVH fusion protein genes.
source: We found that the addition of WT and mutant Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH not only did not affect the average copy number of the corresponding CEN-ARS plasmids in exponentially growing S. cerevisiae cells (Figure 2A), but also even reduced the steady-state transcript levels of the corresponding LacZ-NVH fusion protein genes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The addition of Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH did not result in a significant increase in transcription.
source: Therefore, the addition of Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH did not result in a significant increase in transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing reduced transcript levels

claim: The β-galactosidase activities of Rad51-NTD-LacZ-NVH in WT and all six gene-knockout strains examined were 10- to 29-fold higher than those of LacZ-NVH.
source: We found that the β-galactosidase activities of Rad51-NTD-LacZ-NVH in WT and all six of the gene-knockout strains we examined were 10- to 29-fold higher than those of LacZ-NVH (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The β-galactosidase activities of LacZ-NVH in the six gene-knockout mutants are all lower (30–70%) than those in WT.
source: Intriguingly, the β-galactosidase activities of LacZ-NVH in the six gene-knockout mutants are all lower (30–70%) than those in WT (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The addition of Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH can abrogate the protein homeostasis defects caused by the loss of each of six genes (hsp104, new1, doa1, doa4, san1, oaz1).
source: These results indicate that the addition of Rad51-NTD to LacZ-NVH can abrogate the protein homeostasis defects caused by the loss of each of these six genes.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing rescue of activity in knockout mutants

claim: The PEE activities of Q-rich domains are unlikely to arise from counteracting the N-end rule.
source: For two reasons, the PEE activities of these Q-rich domains are unlikely to arise from counteracting the N-end rule.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of N-terminal amino acid sequences

claim: Rad51-NTD, Rad53-SCD1 and Sup35-NPD exhibit a very strong positive relationship between STQ and STQN amino acid percentages and β-galactosidase activities.
source: We applied an alanine scanning mutagenesis approach to reduce the percentages of S, T, Q, or N in Rad51-NTD, Rad53-SCD1, and Sup35-NPD, respectively. These three Q-rich motifs exhibit a very strong positive relationship between STQ and STQN amino acid percentages and β-galactosidase activities (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5

claim: Rad51-NTD, Rad53-SCD1 and Sup35-NPD are structurally flexible peptides.
source: IUPred2A (https://iupred2a.elte.hu/plot_new), a web-server for identifying disordered protein regions (Mészáros et al., 2018), also revealed that Rad51-NTD, Rad53-SCD1 and Sup35-NPD are structurally flexible peptides.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis using IUPred2A

claim: Q-rich motifs are useful toolkits for creating new diversity during protein evolution.
source: Given that IDRs can endow proteins with structural and functional plasticity (Zhou et al., 2019; Bondos et al., 2022), we hypothesized that Q-rich motifs (e.g. SCD, polyQ and polyQ/N) represent useful toolkits for creating new diversity during protein evolution.
evidence: Hypothesis based on established knowledge about IDRs and the authors' findings

claim: The percentages of SCD proteins in the near-complete proteomes of 21 non-ciliate species and 6 ciliates range from 8.0% in P. falciparum to a maximum of 58.0% in O. trifallax.
source: Our results reveal that the percentages of SCD proteins in the near-complete proteomes of 21 non-ciliate species and 6 ciliates range from 8.0% in P. falciparum, 13.9% in H. sapiens, 16.8% in S. cerevisiae, 24.2% in U. maydis, to a maximum of 58.0% in O. trifallax (Figure 6 and Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: Among the 6050 proteins in the S. cerevisiae reference proteome, 1016 are SCD-hosting proteins.
source: Among the 6050 proteins in the most recently updated S. cerevisiae reference proteome (https://www.uniprot.org/proteomes/UP000002311), we identified 1016 SCD-hosting proteins (Figure 6—source data 2), including all 436 SCD-harboring proteins previously revealed by ScanProsite (Cheung et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of the S. cerevisiae proteome

claim: Q is used more frequently in five unicellular ciliates with reassigned UAAQ and UAGQ codons than in eukaryotes with standard genetic codons.
source: The most striking finding in our study is that, due to their usage of the two noncanonical codons (UAAQ and UAGQ), Q (but not S, T or N) is used more frequently in five unicellular ciliates (i.e. T. thermophila, P. tetraurelia, O. trifallax, S. lemnae, and P. persalinus) than in eukaryotes with standard genetic codons, including the unicellular ciliate S. coeruleus and all of the 20 non-ciliate species we examined herein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Due to higher proteome-wide Q contents, there are higher percentages of SCD, polyQ, and polyQ/N in the five group I ciliates than in S. coeruleus.
source: Due to higher proteome-wide Q contents, there are higher percentages of SCD, polyQ, and polyQ/N in the five group I ciliates than in S. coeruleus (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 2–3, and Figure 6—source data 1–3).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 6 and supplements

claim: Q is used more frequently in group I and group II ciliates than in group III and group IV ciliates or in 20 non-ciliate species.
source: Nevertheless, our results indicate that Q is used more frequently in group I and group II ciliates than in group III and group IV ciliates or in a further 20 non-ciliate species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Proportions of SCD, polyQ and polyQ/N proteins in all group I and group II ciliates are higher than they are in the three group III ciliates (except L. pictus) and the three group IV ciliates.
source: Accordingly, proportions of SCD, polyQ and polyQ/N proteins in all group I and group II ciliates are higher than they are in the three group III ciliates (except L. pictus) and the three group IV ciliates, respectively.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of ciliate proteomes

claim: Y, W, or C are not used more frequently in the three group IV ciliates than in the other 14 ciliate or 20 non-ciliate species.
source: Our data also indicates that Y, W, or C are not used more frequently in the three group IV ciliates than in the other 14 ciliate or 20 non-ciliate species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6—source data 1 file 1).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Reassignments of stop codons to Y, W, or C do not result in higher percentages of polyY, polyW, or polyC proteins in the three group IV ciliates.
source: Reassignments of stop codons to Y, W, or C also do not result in higher percentages of polyY, polyW, or polyC proteins in the three group IV ciliates, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3

claim: The five ciliates with reassigned TAAQ and TAGQ codons have higher Q usage frequency and more polyQ motifs in their proteomes compared to S. coeruleus and several non-ciliate eukaryotic organisms.
source: Most importantly, our results reveal that, compared to S. coeruleus or several non-ciliate eukaryotic organisms (e.g. P. falciparum, C. elegans, D. rerio, M. musculus, and H. sapiens), the five ciliates with reassigned TAAQ and TAGQ codons not only have higher Q usage frequency but also more polyQ motifs in their proteomes (Figure 7 and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 7

claim: PolyQ motifs prevail in C. albicans, C. tropicalis, D. discoideum, C. reinhardtii, D. melanogaster, and A. aegypti, although the Q usage frequencies in their entire proteomes are not significantly higher than those of other eukaryotes.
source: In contrast, polyQ motifs prevail in C. albicans, C. tropicalis, D. discoideum, C. reinhardtii, D. melanogaster, and A. aegypti, although the Q usage frequencies in their entire proteomes are not significantly higher than those of other eukaryotes (Figure 7 and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 7

claim: D. discoideum, P. falciparum, and P. persalinus have more polyN motifs than the other 23 eukaryotes examined due to their higher N usage frequencies.
source: Due to their higher N usage frequencies, D. discoideum, P. falciparum, and P. persalinus have more polyN motifs than the other 23 eukaryotes we examined here (Figure 8 and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: All 26 eukaryotes assessed have similar S usage frequencies and percentages of S contents in polyS motifs.
source: Generally speaking, all 26 eukaryotes we assessed have similar S usage frequencies and percentages of S contents in polyS motifs (Figure 9 and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 9

claim: D. discoideum possesses many more polyT motifs, although its T usage frequency is similar to that of the other 25 eukaryotes.
source: Among these 26 eukaryotes, D. discoideum possesses many more polyT motifs, although its T usage frequency is similar to that of the other 25 eukaryotes (Figure 10 and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 10

claim: The likelihood of forming long CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats is higher in D. melanogaster, D. rerio, M. musculus, H. sapiens, and C. reinhardtii due to their higher CAGQ usage frequencies.
source: Our results reveal that the likelihood of forming long CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats is higher in five eukaryotes due to their higher CAGQ usage frequencies, including D. melanogaster (86.6% Q), D. rerio (74.0% Q), M. musculus (74.0% Q), H. sapiens (73.5% Q), and C. reinhardtii (87.3% Q) (orange background, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Table 2

claim: D. discoideum, C. albicans, C. tropicalis, P. falciparum and S. coeruleus utilize more CAAQ than CAGQ to avoid forming long CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats.
source: In contrast, another five eukaryotes that possess high numbers of polyQ motifs (i.e. D. discoideum, C. albicans, C. tropicalis, P. falciparum and S. coeruleus) (Figure 7) utilize more CAAQ (96.2%, 84.6%, 84.5%, 86.7%, and 75.7%) than CAGQ (3.8%, 15.4%, 15.5%, 13.3%, and 24.3%), respectively, to avoid forming long CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeats (green background, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Table 2

claim: All five ciliates with reassigned stop codons (TAAQ and TAGQ) display low CAGQ usage frequencies ranging from 3.8% Q in P. persalinus to 12.6% Q in O. trifallax.
source: Similarly, all five ciliates with reassigned stop codons (TAAQ and TAGQ) display low CAGQ usage frequencies (i.e. ranging from 3.8% Q in P. persalinus to 12.6% Q in O. trifallax) (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Table 2

claim: Q-rich motifs prevail in proteins involved in specialized biological processes, including S. cerevisiae RNA-mediated transposition, C. albicans filamentous growth, peptidyl-glutamic acid modification in ciliates with reassigned stop codons, T. thermophila xylan catabolism, D. discoideum sexual reproduction, P. falciparum infection, and the nervous systems of D. melanogaster, M. musculus, and H. sapiens.
source: The results presented in Figure 11 and Figure 12, Figure 6—source data 1–31 support the hypothesis that Q-rich motifs prevail in proteins involved in specialized biological processes, including S. cerevisiae RNA-mediated transposition, C. albicans filamentous growth, peptidyl-glutamic acid modification in ciliates with reassigned stop codons (TAAQ and TAGQ), T. thermophila xylan catabolism, D. discoideum sexual reproduction, P. falciparum infection, as well as the nervous systems of D. melanogaster, M. musculus, and H. sapiens.
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 11 and Figure 12

claim: Peptidyl-glutamic acid modification is not overrepresented with Q-rich-motif proteins in S. coeruleus, a ciliate with standard stop codons.
source: In contrast, peptidyl-glutamic acid modification is not overrepresented with Q-rich-motif proteins in S. coeruleus, a ciliate with standard stop codons.
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis

claim: The proteome of T. thermophila contains 58 proteins involved in the xylan catabolic process, of which 56 (97%), 55 (95%), 58 (100%), and 49 (84%) proteins harbor SCD, polyQ, polyQ/N, and polyN tracts, respectively.
source: The proteome of T. thermophila contains 58 proteins involved in the xylan catabolic process (GO ID: 45493), of which 56 (97%), 55 (95%), 58 (100%), and 49 (84%) proteins harbor SCD, polyQ, polyQ/N, and polyN tracts, respectively (Figure 6—source data 18–23).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of T. thermophila proteome

claim: T. thermophila has more abundant xylan catabolic proteins than all other ciliates examined.
source: Using the NCBI BLASTP search tool with an expect value (E-value) ≤10e-5 to search for homologs of these 58 proteins among all the other 16 ciliates analyzed in this study, we only identified 144 proteins with amino acid identity >60% and a raw alignment score of >150 (Figure 6—source data 32). Thus, T. thermophila has more abundant xylan catabolic proteins than all other ciliates we examined herein.
evidence: Supported by BLASTP analysis

claim: Among the 124 T. thermophila meiotic proteins, 85 are SCD proteins, 54 are polyQ proteins, 106 are polyQ/N proteins, 32 are polyN proteins, 32 are polyS proteins, and 48 are polyK proteins.
source: Among the 124 T. thermophila meiotic proteins (Figure 6—source data 33, see review in Loidl, 2021), we identified 85 SCD proteins, 54 polyQ proteins, 106 polyQ/N proteins, 32 polyN proteins, 32 polyS proteins, and 48 polyK proteins, respectively.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of T. thermophila meiotic proteins

claim: There are 48 and 59 T. thermophila meiotic proteins that contain ≥4 SCDs and/or ≥4 polyQ/N tracts, respectively.
source: Notably, there are 48 and 59 meiotic proteins that contain ≥4 SCDs and/or ≥4 polyQ/N tracts, respectively.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of T. thermophila meiotic proteins

claim: The Q-rich motifs in most (if not all) T. thermophila meiotic proteins are intrinsically disordered.
source: Using IUPred2A (https://iupred2a.elte.hu/plot_new), we found that the Q-rich motifs in most (if not all) of these meiotic proteins are intrinsically disordered.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis using IUPred2A

claim: The Q-rich motifs in T. thermophila meiotic proteins might form tunable proteinaceous condensates to regulate assembly and disassembly of the 'crescents' in ciliate MICs.
source: Accordingly, we speculate that, like the C-terminal IDR of mammalian CTTNBP2, the Q-rich motifs in T. thermophila meiotic proteins might form tunable proteinaceous condensates to regulate assembly and disassembly of the 'crescents' in ciliate MICs.
evidence: Speculative inference based on analogy to CTTNBP2

claim: The reassignment of stop codons to Q in the group I and group II ciliates significantly increases proteome-wide Q usage, leading to massive expansion of structurally flexible or even intrinsically disordered Q-rich motifs.
source: Second, the reassignment of stop codons to Q in the group I and group II ciliates significantly increases proteome-wide Q usage, leading to massive expansion of structurally flexible or even intrinsically disordered Q-rich motifs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from computational analysis of ciliate proteomes

claim: Reassignments of stop codons to Y, W, or C do not result in higher usages of these three amino acid residues, nor higher percentages of W-, Y-, or C-rich proteins in the three group IV ciliates.
source: In contrast, reassignments of stop codons to Y, W, or C do not result in higher usages of these three amino acid residues, nor higher percentages of W-, Y-, or C-rich proteins in the three group IV ciliates, respectively.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from computational analysis of ciliate proteomes

claim: A decrease or increase of CAGQ usage frequency in different eukaryotes is responsible for a reduction or augmentation, respectively, of polyQ instability (or expansion) caused by DNA strand slippage in CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeat regions during DNA replication.
source: Third, the results in Table 2 support that a decrease or increase of CAGQ usage frequency in different eukaryotes is responsible for a reduction or augmentation, respectively, of polyQ instability (or expansion) caused by DNA strand slippage in CAG/CTG trinucleotide repeat regions during DNA replication (Petruska et al., 1998; Mier and Andrade-Navarro, 2021).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from computational analysis shown in Table 2 and supported by citations

claim: Q-rich motifs can endow proteins with structural and functional plasticity.
source: Due to their structural flexibility, Q-rich motifs can endow proteins with structural and functional plasticity.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the study's findings and prior literature

claim: Q-rich motifs are useful toolkits for generating novel diversity during protein evolution.
source: Based on previous reports (Zhou et al., 2019; Bondos et al., 2022) and our findings from this study, Q-rich motifs, such as IDRs, are useful toolkits for generating novel diversity during protein evolution, including by enabling greater protein expression, protein-protein interactions, posttranslational modifications, increased solubility, and tunable stability, among other important traits.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings and supported by citations

claim: Due to higher Q usage, many proteins involved in evolutionarily conserved biological processes in group I and group II ciliates display more diverse amino acid sequences than the respective proteins in other ciliate or non-ciliate species.
source: First, due to higher Q usage, many proteins involved in evolutionarily conserved biological processes in group I and group II ciliates display more diverse amino acid sequences than the respective proteins in other ciliate or non-ciliate species.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study's findings

claim: It is sometimes difficult to identify authentic protein homologs among different ciliates, particularly for group I and group II ciliates.
source: Accordingly, it is sometimes difficult to identify authentic protein homologs among different ciliates, particularly for group I and group II ciliates.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation of diverse amino acid sequences

claim: Structurally flexible Q-rich motifs might form various membraneless organelles or proteinaceous condensates via intracellular liquid-liquid phase separation in tunable manners.
source: In theory, structurally flexible Q-rich motifs might form various membraneless organelles or proteinaceous condensates via intracellular liquid-liquid phase separation in tunable manners, including protein posttranslational modification, protein-protein interaction, protein-ligand binding, among other processes (Wright and Dyson, 1999; Posey et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citations

claim: The C-terminus of mouse CTTNBP2 facilitates co-condensation of CTTNBP2 with SHANK3 at the postsynaptic density in a Zn2+-dependent manner.
source: A typical example is that the C-terminus of mouse CTTNBP2 facilitates co-condensation of CTTNBP2 with SHANK3 at the postsynaptic density in a Zn2+-dependent manner (Shih et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Distinct evolutionary strategies are employed in different species to alter protein regions that are structurally flexible or even intrinsically disordered.
source: Accordingly, distinct evolutionary strategies are employed in different species to alter protein regions that are structurally flexible or even intrinsically disordered.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study's findings and comparison with Borgs

claim: Glutamine (Q) is used more frequently in all 10 ciliate species possessing reassigned TAAQ and TAGQ codons than in other ciliates and non-ciliate species.
source: Here, we show that glutamine (Q) is used more frequently in all 10 ciliate species possessing reassigned TAAQ and TAGQ codons than in other ciliates and non-ciliate species.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from computational analysis of ciliate proteomes

claim: The consequence of the preponderance of Q in ciliates with reassigned stop codons is the massive expansion of proteins harboring structurally flexible or even intrinsically disordered Q-rich motifs.
source: The consequence of this preponderance of Q is the massive expansion of proteins harboring structurally flexible or even intrinsically disordered Q-rich motifs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from computational analysis of ciliate proteomes

claim: Q-rich-motif proteins are overrepresented in several species-specific or even phylum-specific biological processes.
source: Since Q-rich motifs can endow proteins with structural and functional plasticity and Q-rich-motif proteins are overrepresented in several species-specific or even phylum-specific biological processes, we suggest that Q-rich motifs are useful toolkits for evolutionary novelty.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from GO enrichment analysis
